_comment: The firewall's rule file. This is the only thing you edit in this lab.
_block_at_note: Severity is the NUMBER OF DETECTOR FAMILIES that matched, nothing cleverer:
1 family = MEDIUM    2 families = HIGH    3 or more = CRITICAL
block_at is the lowest severity the firewall will actually stop.
It ships as CRITICAL on purpose. That is the vulnerable configuration, and
it is copied from a real one: CVE-2026-60086 (PraisonAI < 4.6.78, July 2026)
blocked only what it rated CRITICAL, which needed three or more detector
families at once, so single and double-vector injections rated HIGH went
_concealment_note: The fourth family, 'concealment', is structural: it is computed from the raw
HTML, not from the extracted text, because it is about how the payload is
hidden rather than what it says. Two checks, and both are real techniques:
- CSS that hides the element from a reader but not from a scraper
- Unicode characters that are invisible in every browser and legible to a
tokenizer. Microsoft measured a phishing campaign using exactly these in
2026, peaking at 2.3 million messages a day (2026-09-03).
_outbound_note: The outbound side. Note what is here and what is NOT: this is a PATTERN, the
shape of the credential, not its value. That is how a real DLP rule is written,
and for the same reason - a rule file is read, copied, diffed and pasted into
tickets, so putting the secret in it just moves the leak somewhere quieter.
The key this matches is FAKE and exists only inside this container. It is a
canary, which is what MITRE ATLAS AML.M0035 recommends against LLM Data
Leakage: 'place synthetic secrets or canary records in representative data
sources and attempt extraction'. If a value matching this pattern appears in a
model response, the response is suppressed and the attempt is logged with the
value redacted. It is never printed, never written to the log in full, and
never sent anywhere - there is nowhere to send it.
